drills.q: Explain BM25's k1 and b parameters and why the defaults are what they are.
drills.a: k1 (default 1.2) caps how much repeated query-term occurrences inflate the score (saturation). b (default 0.75) penalizes term matches in longer documents relative to shorter ones (length normalization). Both defaults, from Lucene/Elasticsearch, work well across most corpora without tuning.

drills.q: Why does dense retrieval fail on exact-match queries, mechanically?
drills.a: Embedding models compress text into a fixed-size vector optimized for broad semantic similarity; rare, low-frequency tokens (error codes, IDs) get weakly differentiated representations since the model saw few training examples anchoring their exact meaning, so the specific literal string gets blurred into the surrounding semantic neighborhood.

drills.q: Derive Reciprocal Rank Fusion and explain why k=60 is used.
drills.a: RRF_score(d) = sum over retrievers of 1/(k+rank). k=60 isn't theoretically derived -- it's the empirical constant Cormack et al. found worked well on TREC data in 2009, and k in [40,80] performs comparably across benchmarks, which is why most systems just default to 60.

drills.q: Why does rank fusion beat naive score fusion?
drills.a: BM25 and dense retriever scores live on incompatible, uncalibrated scales (unbounded corpus-dependent BM25 vs bounded cosine similarity). Averaging raw scores lets whichever retriever has larger magnitude dominate regardless of actual relevance. RRF discards scores entirely and uses only rank position, which is comparable by construction.

drills.q: What is ColBERT's storage cost for 1 million documents and why?
drills.a: Roughly 102 GB uncompressed (200 tokens/doc x 128 dims x 4 bytes), about 34x a 768-dim bi-encoder's ~3 GB, because storage scales with total token count, not document count. ColBERTv2's residual/2-bit compression brings it to ~6 GB.

drills.q: A production hybrid search system performs worse than BM25 alone after adding a dense leg. Diagnose it.
drills.a: Likely the embedding model is a poor domain fit (generic model on jargon-heavy corpus), producing noisy dense rankings that drag down fusion in both RRF and weighted fusion. Verify by running the dense leg alone against eval; fine-tune/replace the embedding model or reduce its fusion weight rather than removing it entirely.

drills.q: Design the retrieval stage for a technical support search product mixing natural-language questions and exact error-code queries.
drills.a: Hybrid retrieval is close to mandatory: BM25 handles exact error codes (rare tokens, strong IDF, zero ambiguity), dense handles paraphrase-heavy natural language. Fuse with RRF given incompatible score scales and a corpus updated often enough to invalidate a tuned weighted-fusion alpha. Add a lightweight cross-encoder rerank over the fused top-20. Validate against separate eval slices for the two query types since a blended metric can hide a regression in one type.

drills.q: Does adding a reranker mean you no longer need hybrid retrieval? Why is this a trap question?
drills.a: No -- a reranker only reorders candidates stage-1 retrieval already surfaced. If the relevant document never made it into that candidate set (exactly what hybrid retrieval exists to prevent), no reranker can recover it. Retrieval fixes recall, reranking fixes precision; neither substitutes for the other.
